The Edge of Change
3.4 · التصميم والتطور · Design & EvolutionSource: God’s Undertaker↑ Contents

The Nature and Scope of Evolution

John C. Lennox · God’s Undertaker: Has Science Buried God? · Chapter 6

In This Chapter — The Argument Map

  1. Untangle the five meanings covered by the word evolution.
  2. Distinguish the selective preservation of variation from its initial production.
  3. Trace the proposed limits of mutation and selection, including the evidence and probability arguments.
  4. Examine fossil stasis, sudden appearance and the intermediate/transitional distinction.
  5. Separate genetic relatedness from its causal explanation; follow the thought experiment about Smith and the conclusion about Logos.
“But selection has no innovative capacity: it eliminates or maintains what exists.”Gerd Müller, quoted by John C. Lennox, p. 105
Central thesis

Lennox accepts that mutation and selection account for much observed variation. He asks how far that success extends. His case turns on limits to extrapolation: evidence that a mechanism changes what already lives does not by itself explain major innovations, the extent of genetic relatedness, or the first life. He argues that evolutionary biology does not entail atheism and that the evidence points to intelligent input.

§I What does “evolution” mean?

This section answers: Which claim is being made when one word names several processes or outcomes?

Lennox separates five uses of evolution. Change says nothing about its cause; microevolution names limited variation in existing structures. Macroevolution concerns new organs, body plans or qualitatively new genetic material. Artificial selection involves deliberate choice. Molecular evolution can mean the emergence of life, whereas Darwinian selection requires mutating replicators.

The Galápagos finch changes reversed when rains returned. Lennox also discusses the peppered moth story, whose particulars Michael Majerus questioned. Even if the story holds, a change in the proportions of two kinds of moth already present is not the arrival of a new form. E. O. Wilson’s bird eye colours pose the same problem: changing frequencies do not explain where the birds came from.

Source depthWhat was at issue in the textbook story?Optional detail

What was at issue in the textbook story?

The familiar account links colour frequencies to predators spotting light moths against dark, polluted tree trunks. Lennox reports doubts about where the moths rest in the wild and notes controversy about staged illustrations. He distinguishes these points from his argument that both colour forms were already present.

John C. Lennox, God’s Undertaker: Has Science Buried God?, pp. 101–102.

Read the claim before assessing its evidence
UseWhat it commits the speaker to
Change or developmentA motor car and a coastline both change; the word by itself does not say what caused either change.
MicroevolutionExisting traits vary, for instance when finch beak lengths change. A later reversal can show that selection is real without showing permanent progress.
MacroevolutionNew forms or structures originate. The gradualist must still show that processes observed on the smaller scale can account for them.
Artificial selectionBreeders deliberately choose, as with roses and sheep. Lennox denies that this analogy by itself establishes unguided evolution.
Molecular evolutionA term for the emergence of the living cell from nonliving material. Dobzhansky’s point concerns the absence of the mutating replicators that selection needs.

§II What natural selection does

This section answers: Does a rule for retaining advantageous differences explain where they came from?

Colin Patterson derives differential success from reproduction, inherited differences and the effects of those differences on reproduction. Lennox takes selection in that sense to be a necessary consequence of the premises, not a claim that selection explains every feature. He draws the same line with Gerd Müller: loss or preservation of a part is not the production or organization of the part.

Dawkins does not appeal to chance alone: selection is supposed to retain useful chance variations and shorten the search. Lennox asks what happens when scarcity of resources is lifted. If more offspring survive, there is less for selection to eliminate. Hooker had pressed the same distinction: variation could generate differences without selection creating them. Darwin agreed in principle, with conditions about adaptation and the preservation of variations against intercrossing.

Source depthDarwin’s qualifications to HookerOptional detail

Darwin’s qualifications to Hooker

Darwin’s reply stipulates that forms can remain adapted to conditions long enough, while conditions can change in the long run. He also stipulates self-fertilization to prevent fine variations from being lost through intercrossing. He accepts that the breeder selects a modification without producing it, but defends his own emphasis on selection because it helped explain adaptation.

John C. Lennox, God’s Undertaker: Has Science Buried God?, pp. 105–107.

Patterson’s deductive argument
Premise 1
Organisms reproduce and generate descendants.
Premise 2
Their differences can be inherited.
Premise 3
Those differences do not all have the same effects on reproductive success.
Consequence
Differences that favour reproductive success spread relative to the others. This follows without a premise that selection is the only cause of evolutionary change.
Do not mistake a label for an explanation

Patterson accepts differential reproductive success. What he questions is the unrestricted use of selection to explain every feature. Lennox reads this as a warning: an explanation that covers every possible outcome needs more than the label of selection to establish why this particular outcome occurred.

🎨
Study analogy: judging an exhibition

A judge can change which pictures hang in a gallery by keeping some and removing others. Judging does not paint a picture that was absent. This illustrates the limited meaning of selection under discussion; it is not an analogy for the whole biology of an evolving population.

§III Testing the reach of mutation and selection

This section answers: Where does the evidence end, and what does Behe infer beyond it?

The boundary between microevolution and macroevolution is disputed. Lennox asks whether the processes that change beaks or produce resistance account for the origin of finches and bacteria. He cites Scherer’s classification by hybridization and Grassé’s reports of variation reaching limits in breeding. He then reports Behe’s interpretation of long-running bacterial studies: adaptation can involve the loss of machinery rather than the construction of new machinery.

Behe treats historical malaria research as a test case because the populations were enormous. He credits observed resistance as an instance of Darwinian change but estimates the rarity of the chloroquine-resistance event and calls a cluster of that degree a CCC. He expects no double CCC from the mechanism over the history of life, and argues that biological regulatory systems exceed this proposed limit. The claim about that wider range is an extrapolation, not another observation of resistance.

Source depthBehe’s analogy with the search for the etherOptional detail

Behe’s analogy with the search for the ether

Behe compares the very large natural trials represented by disease histories with a historical test in physics. In his account, finding small changes but no new coherent machinery in those trials counts against the proposed creative reach of the mechanism. Lennox presents this as Behe’s interpretation of the data, not as a laboratory demonstration of the origin of life.

John C. Lennox, God’s Undertaker: Has Science Buried God?, pp. 110–111.

Different evidence for different parts of the edge argument
CaseWhat Lennox uses it to ask
Hybridization and breedingScherer’s proposed basic type may include more than one species and does not require fertile hybrids. Grassé calls attention to limits to the variation breeders can obtain.
Bacterial populationsDoes a change that helps a bacterium under the conditions studied amount to building a comparably elaborate new system? Behe interprets some changes as losses that reduce costs.
Chloroquine-resistance comparisonBehe gives about one in 10²⁰ for the event he discusses. That figure belongs to this case. For the same rarity, a much smaller population would offer fewer opportunities and a longer expected wait.
Further coordinationBehe draws a separate conclusion about a hypothetical double CCC and invokes genetic regulatory networks as an example of structures he thinks go beyond the proposed edge.
How to state a probability claim

Name the event, who estimates its rarity and what opportunities are counted. Then identify the extra step from that event to a claim about a more complex change. Do not use Behe’s estimate as the odds of evolution in general.

§IV What the mathematicians disputed

This section answers: When should a calculation test a proposed explanation rather than be rejected by it?

At the 1966 Wistar meeting, Stanley Ulam argued that the time available was too short for the eye to emerge under his model of gradual changes. Peter Medawar countered that the eye’s evolution exposed a flaw in the model. Lennox objects that presupposing the conclusion can prevent the calculation from testing the account. Schützenberger supported Ulam’s challenge but rejected the claim that he was arguing for special creation. Hoyle likewise distinguished a theory’s success within the range of observations from its validity outside that range.

What the mathematical dispute does and does not concern

The dispute is not whether every useful observation behind Darwin’s theory should be abandoned. Hoyle accepts that a theory may be valid inside the range of those observations. The question is where extrapolation stops being warranted and why. Lennox takes disagreement about the model as reason to keep that question open to scrutiny.

§V What a fossil can establish

This section answers: How do stasis, sudden appearance and intermediate features bear differently on gradualism?

Darwin expected numerous intermediate varieties and recognized their scarcity in the available strata as an objection. Lennox cites later palaeontologists on long stasis and relatively sudden local appearance. Gould and Eldredge proposed punctuated equilibrium to account for the pattern, and Gould cited the Cambrian appearance of many major groups. Lennox asks what mechanism could produce the comparatively rapid changes.

An intermediate can sit between two groups in a classification without being on their actual ancestral line. Lennox uses Archaeopteryx in that distinction. He recognizes incomplete preservation but follows Valentine in denying that it accounts for all missing ancestries. Conway Morris also allows that small genetic changes might trigger large changes of form once sufficiently complex organisms exist, while stressing how poorly the link between code and form is understood.

Source depthTwo qualifications in the fossil discussionOptional detail

Two qualifications in the fossil discussion

Valentine grants that fossil preservation can leave breaks in a lineage, but denies that it accounts for all such cases. Lennox also recounts Paul Chien and colleagues’ question about exceptionally preserved Precambrian embryos: why are the precursors to Cambrian animals not present where soft tissue can sometimes survive?

John C. Lennox, God’s Undertaker: Has Science Buried God?, p. 116.

🎞️
Study analogy: classifying frames and proving the sequence

Still frames can be arranged from a less open to a more open door, but that order is not proof that they came from the same sequence. Lennox’s distinction concerns the extra evidence needed to move from an intermediate appearance to a particular historical claim.

Stasis and sudden appearance

Stasis is the persistence of similar form across a long interval. Sudden appearance describes how a form first shows up in the local fossil record, not an explanation of what brought it about. Punctuated equilibrium takes the pairing of relative stability and comparatively rapid change seriously.

§VI Genetic relatedness, design and Logos

This section answers: What remains to be shown after a genetic similarity has been established?

For Lennox, an unobserved and unrepeatable origin is not established in the same way as the repeatedly observed orbit of the earth. He considers genetic relatedness a serious objection to the proposed edge. He accepts the similarities but denies that they identify mutation and selection as the sole causes. A design can be shared, as with cars, and common ancestry and design need not exclude each other.

In the Smith thought experiment, a future researcher observes genetically related wheat but dismisses a record of deliberate alteration. The relatedness survives either reading. Lennox says the possibility of intentional input does not establish supernatural input: that requires further evidence. He presents Meyer’s comparison of the two historical hypotheses, Behe’s positive appeal to molecular organization, and Nagel’s judgment that the evidence does not rule out intelligence.

Source depthWhy call this a historical comparison?Optional detail

Why call this a historical comparison?

Lennox reports Stephen Meyer’s point that common design and common ancestry both appeal to proposed causes not directly observed in the past. He presents that as a comparison of their standing as historical explanations, not as a proof that either proposed history occurred.

John C. Lennox, God’s Undertaker: Has Science Buried God?, pp. 119–120.

Collins and Conway Morris need not accept Behe’s edge to question an ultimately unguided account. Conway Morris points to the recurring convergence of life on similar solutions; Collins calls his account BioLogos. Lennox concludes that a worldview does not follow logically from a science, that the observed success of mutation and selection does not explain all life’s variety, and that the origin of a replicator is the distinct and harder problem.

Two different reasons in the conclusion

The distinction between a science and a worldview is Lennox’s logical reason not to deduce atheism. His further, evidential argument compares the organization and regulation of living systems with the fine-tuned physical universe. These, he thinks, bear marks of intelligence; their presence is not itself a proposal for the first replicator’s origin.

From observation to explanatory claim
Observed genetic similarityraises the question ofits historical cause
Common ancestryneed not excludeintentional direction
Smith’s wheatillustrates a limit onwhat relatedness rules out
Evolution of living thingspresupposesan already existing replicator
Trace the transitions
  • Use the finches to say what the observation supports, then identify the different argument needed for a claim about the origin of birds.
  • Give the reasoning that leads from Patterson’s premises to differential success. Explain why a rule for retaining a variant is not an explanation of its production.
  • Identify where Behe moves from the observed case to a probability estimate and then to a proposed wider limit. What are the different evidential jobs of the three steps?
  • What does Smith’s record contribute beyond the genetic similarity? Why can it not by itself establish the stronger claim that Lennox discusses?

Revision Block · Dossier 3.4.8

Chapter Summary

Lennox separates five senses of evolution. He accepts ordinary variation and the selective success of inherited differences; he asks whether they explain the origin of major innovations. With Hooker, Patterson and Müller he distinguishes the production of a form from its selective retention. He considers breeding, microbial observations and Behe’s estimate for resistance, then examines how mathematical models and the fossil record bear on claims of gradual innovation. He treats genetic similarity as evidence to be explained rather than a verdict on whether intelligence was involved. He closes by separating mutation and selection, which require a replicator, from the problem of the origin of life.

One-Page Revision Sheet

MeaningChange, limited inherited variation, major innovation, artificial selection and the emergence of life are different claims.
MechanismReproduction, inheritance and unequal success explain why some variants become more common, not why the variants first arose.
ResourcesAs more offspring survive, the filtering effect in Lennox’s limiting case weakens.
BreedingScherer groups by hybridization; Grassé emphasizes limits on breeding variation.
EdgeBreeding limits, bacterial studies and Behe’s historical malaria comparison are different pieces of evidence about the reach of a mechanism.
ExtrapolationThe validity of a model within its observed range is distinct from its validity outside that range.
FossilsStasis and relatively sudden appearance motivate punctuated equilibrium. A morphological intermediate is not necessarily a demonstrated ancestor.
RelatednessSimilarities do not show by themselves whether only undirected causes were involved. Smith illustrates the distinction.
ObservationLennox distinguishes repeated observation of an orbit from an inference about an unrepeatable origin.
ConclusionCollins and Conway Morris can differ from Behe about the edge without embracing an ultimately purposeless account. Selection does not explain its own first replicator.

Key Definitions

Microevolution
In this chapter, variation within an existing range of complexity.
Macroevolution
In this chapter, the origin of major biological novelty.
Natural selection
Differential reproductive success among inherited variants.
Basic type
Scherer’s grouping by direct or indirect hybridization, whether hybrids are fertile or not.
Genetic homeostasis
Here, the tendency for further variation to meet barriers as a gene pool is subjected to breeding.
CCC
Behe’s name for a cluster comparable in complexity to the one in his chloroquine-resistance example.
Stasis
Relative stability of form in the fossil record.
Intermediate form
A form between two groups in a classification; not thereby a demonstrated transitional ancestor.
BioLogos
Collins’s term for his account, life through Logos.
Punctuated equilibrium
Gould and Eldredge’s account of long stasis punctuated by comparatively rapid changes.
Cryptogenic gap
A gap where the ancestry of a branch cannot be traced, in Valentine’s discussion.
Artificial selection
Deliberate breeding in which a chooser retains some variants rather than others.

Key Table — Meaning and evidence

Use §I to fix the sense of evolution before stating what a case supports. Use §III to distinguish variation or adaptation that was observed from the wider limits that the quoted authors infer. §V and §VI apply the same discipline to the difference between a classificatory observation and an account of origins.

Memory Aids Collected

  • Five meanings: name the process or claim before appraising the evidence.
  • The gallery: selecting from pictures and painting one are different jobs.
  • One estimate: Behe assigns a rarity to a particular event, not to every biological innovation.
  • Film frames: an arrangement by resemblance does not establish an actual sequence.
  • Smith: the record changes the history entertained, not the similarity seen.

Possible Examination Questions

  2. State Patterson’s three premises and the consequence he draws from them.

  2. How does Lennox use the fossil and genetic evidence before presenting his own conclusion?

  2. Compare the evidence needed to classify a fossil as intermediate with the evidence needed to establish ancestry.

  2. Why does the problem of the first replicator remain when selection has been explained?

  2. In the Smith thought experiment, what can the observer infer before and after recovering the record?

The Information Chasm
3.4 · التصميم والتطور · Design & EvolutionSource: The Origin of Life↑ Contents

The Origin of Life

Original author: John C. Lennox · God’s Undertaker: Has Science Buried God?, chapter 7

In This Chapter — The Argument Map

  1. Begin with the molecular organization shared by known living cells.
  2. Distinguish Behe’s design inference from Lennox’s account of the controversy.
  3. Follow the origin question from early atmospheric chemistry to bonds and sequence.
  4. Compare chemical self-organization with the formation of a hereditary system.
  5. Distinguish order imposed by physical conditions from genetically directed organization.
“Between a living cell and the most highly ordered non-biological systems, such as a crystal or a snowflake, there is a chasm as vast and absolute as it is possible to conceive.”Michael Denton, quoted by John C. Lennox, chapter 7 opening leaf
CCentral idea — From order to information

Lennox starts with the machinery of living cells and asks how the information on which that machinery relies could have originated. He grants that natural processes can produce regular patterns. His question is whether that regularity explains the particular sequences and internal direction of living systems. The chapter ends with researchers’ accounts of what remains unexplained, not with a demonstration of how the first cell arose.

§IThe discontinuity between a cell and a crystal

This section answers: What makes Denton’s factory comparison different from a claim about how many atoms a cell contains?

Lennox opens with Stuart Kauffman’s view that life’s origin is unknown and Anthony Flew’s account of the difficulty of a naturalistic theory of the first reproducer. Lennox starts with cellular machinery before narrowing the question to DNA.

Michael Denton contrasts a cell’s machinery with crystal or snowflake symmetry. He stresses the shared biochemical plan of bacteria and mammals: roles for DNA, messenger RNA and proteins, the meaning of the code and the machinery that translates it. Jacques Monod says the simplest known cells do not show what a primitive cell was like. Lennox calls this similarity cellular stasis, paralleling the previous chapter’s fossil discussion.

Source DepthHow uniform is the biochemical plan?Optional source detail

How uniform is the biochemical plan?

Denton distinguishes identical roles for DNA, messenger RNA and protein from the virtually identical meanings of the code and the practical similarity of the protein-making machinery. Monod’s example is that bacterial and human cells work from the same overall chemical plan despite their enormous differences in scale and appearance.

John C. Lennox, God’s Undertaker: Has Science Buried God?, ch. 7, p. 123.

Denton’s contrast: regular shape and coordinated work
What to comparePhysical patternLiving cell
What is ordered?A crystal or snowflake displays a regular arrangement.Many different molecular assemblies carry out interdependent tasks.
What does the comparison show?Order can exist without the machinery used in a living cell.Denton’s figure of roughly 100 billion atoms indicates scale; the factory comparison adds coordination.
What is still unknown?Regularity alone does not describe a path to a first cell.Monod’s comparison of bacteria with other cells does not tell us what the first cell looked like.

§IIInterlocking parts and the scope of Behe’s claim

This section answers: What does the removal of one part establish in Behe’s argument, and what remains disputed?

Bruce Alberts likens cellular protein machines to linked assembly lines. Michael Behe describes the bacterial flagellum’s motor as an assembly of about forty protein parts. He calls a system irreducibly complex if removing a necessary interacting part effectively stops its basic function. His mousetrap illustrates why such an incomplete precursor could not develop directly through improvements to the same working mechanism.

Source DepthHow Gould uses the idea of complexityOptional source detail

How Gould uses the idea of complexity

Stephen Jay Gould contrasts simple systems, such as planetary motion, with complex phenomena in biology, society and history. He calls for new philosophies and models drawing on science and the humanities. Lennox cites the methodological claim without suggesting that Gould shared Behe’s design inference.

John C. Lennox, God’s Undertaker: Has Science Buried God?, ch. 7, pp. 124, 125.

Dawkins echoes Darwin’s test: demonstrate an organ could not arise by successive slight modifications. Proving irreducibility, Lennox says, is difficult because it requires proving a negative. He cites James Shapiro and Behe’s critic Cavalier-Smith on the absence of detailed biochemical models, and Stephen Jay Gould on limits to explaining complexity by a few factors. Behe does not dispute descent with modification as such. He argues that neo-Darwinism cannot explain irreducible complexity and that design follows from the data, not scripture. Lennox leaves open whether Behe has established his case.

🪤
Source analogy — What is lost when a part is removed?

Picture Behe’s mousetrap without its spring. The question is not whether the remaining pieces exist or might be of use elsewhere. It is whether the mechanism still traps mice. Apply that same question to the function Behe names in the motor: swimming. This is the reasoning behind his claim about a direct route through working predecessors.

✕Keep three claims apart

Darwin states what would defeat his theory. Behe argues that biochemical machines meet the challenge and are evidence of design. Lennox reports both the inference and the continuing controversy over whether it has been established. Shapiro and Cavalier-Smith’s statements about missing detailed accounts are not endorsements of Behe’s conclusion.

§IIIBuilding blocks, bonding and the time available

This section answers: What does producing amino acids establish before the work of making a useful protein begins?

Dawkins’s replicator-first proposal begins with a molecule that arises by chance and can copy itself. The metabolism-first proposal starts with energy-driven chemistry before heredity. Lennox then asks how the materials for a living system could arise.

Stanley Miller tested A. I. Oparin’s picture of a strongly reducing early atmosphere and obtained amino acids. Lennox argues that later evidence about atmospheric composition, including evidence he cites for oxygen, points instead to conditions hostile to forming and preserving amino acids. He separates selecting the required handedness from forming the needed bonds. Chirality means mirror-image molecular form; most natural proteins use the L form. Reproducible folding also requires peptide bonds. Cells maintain both conditions with machinery not yet available before life.

Source DepthWhy Lennox compares two small probabilitiesOptional source detail

Why Lennox compares two small probabilities

Lennox compares the estimates for handedness and bonding to the much earlier discussion of fine-tuning. He suggests that even the chemistry required before the formation of a full cell might invite a similar inference. His comparison is not another estimate of the chance that life began.

John C. Lennox, God’s Undertaker: Has Science Buried God?, ch. 7, p. 127.

Paul Davies adds a thermodynamic difficulty. In closed systems entropy tends to increase, making spontaneous peptide assembly unlikely, not impossible. Lennox estimates less than a billion years between Earth’s formation and evidence of single-celled life.

What each step adds to the preceding one
QuestionWhy Lennox treats it separately
Can building blocks form?Lennox reports Miller’s 2 percent yield of amino acids and that later work produced all but one of the twenty. The result depends on the atmosphere assumed. Lennox asks whether that atmosphere was present on early Earth and whether its products could persist.
Are the forms compatible?The existence of amino acids does not supply the same handedness across the chain. Lennox models one hundred L selections at roughly one chance in 1030.
Are the links compatible?The existence of the right forms does not supply the right bonds. Lennox’s comparable bond estimate gives a joint illustration of about one chance in 1060 under his assumptions.
Can a chain assemble in time?Davies’s difficulty concerns the direction of spontaneous change. Lennox adds a time constraint on any proposed process, not a new prohibition in thermodynamics.
DThree different selection questions

Handedness asks which form of a building block is present; bonding asks how blocks are linked. Neither tells us which amino acid occupies which place in the finished chain. That last question introduces sequence.

§IVWhat the order of a protein adds

This section answers: Why is a collection of the correct ingredients not yet an arrangement that works?

For Lennox, the largest problem is arrangement. Davies’s bricks and dynamite show why energy alone does not direct construction. A. G. Cairns-Smith compares letters and short words with a much longer ordered sequence. Treating the twenty amino acids as an alphabet, Lennox estimates the chance of one specified hundred-position sequence under uniform independent choices: (1/20)100, about one in 10130.

Source DepthThe larger estimate reported after the protein modelOptional source detail

The larger estimate reported after the protein model

Lennox moves from the illustration of one specified chain to the much larger problem of getting the many proteins used in life. He reports odds against producing these proteins by chance of more than 1040,000 to one and then introduces Hoyle’s airplane. The reported figure and the simple one-chain calculation are distinct.

John C. Lennox, God’s Undertaker: Has Science Buried God?, ch. 7, pp. 128, 129.

Fred Hoyle’s tornado and Boeing 747 and Cicero’s account of Balbus scattering golden letters distinguish available parts from a working or meaningful arrangement. Lennox rejects blind chance as the explanation, then considers self-organization.

Track the event before reading the number
Alphabet
Lennox assigns twenty possible amino acids to each position. The model gives one wanted choice at that position.
Sequence
The calculation repeats that choice one hundred times. It targets one specified order, not merely a chain of the right length.
Result
The result is about one in 10130 for that event under the model. It is not the earlier calculation about handedness and bonds.
🔤
Source analogy — Balbus’s scattered letters

Balbus, in Cicero’s account, imagines casting copies of the alphabet made of gold onto the ground and asking whether they would yield the Annals of Ennius. Gold is not the missing ingredient. The test is whether the letters fall into an order that forms even a verse. In the protein example, position likewise matters to the result.

§VWhat self-organization can show

This section answers: How do pattern-forming systems differ from the metabolism-first proposal they are used to motivate?

Ilya Prigogine and Isabelle Stengers describe systems driven far from equilibrium in which small changes can have large effects and unexpected order can arise. Lennox contrasts the spatial pattern of Rayleigh–Bénard convection with the Belousov–Zhabotinski chemical clock. In his simplified account, competing reactions and positive feedback produce alternating colours.

Robert Shapiro’s metabolism-first scenario starts with energy-driven chemical cycles. Leslie Orgel argues that catalysts for the wanted reactions are necessary but not sufficient because competing reactions could disrupt the cycle. Carefully designed laboratory inputs do not explain how the same inputs would arise unprepared. Orgel contrasts the complex mixtures yielded in prebiotic simulations with the relatively pure inputs that replication schemes require. He says that simplifying product mixtures or finding very simple replicating polymers would help close that gap.

Source DepthSpecificity rather than speedOptional source detail

Specificity rather than speed

Orgel’s example is the reverse citric acid cycle. He allows that a suitable mineral might exist for a particular step, but doubts that a full set would be present together without materials that promote disruptive side reactions. A reaction being slow is a different problem from it favouring the wrong products.

John C. Lennox, God’s Undertaker: Has Science Buried God?, ch. 7, pp. 131, 132.

DPositive feedback in a chemical clock

In the chapter’s simplified example, one product helps its own production, so its increase can itself increase the rate. Another reaction eventually reduces that product. As their relative effects change, the dominant colour changes too. The recurring result is a temporal pattern. It does not yet explain heredity or how a chemical system would store functional instructions.

★What Orgel is testing

Asking whether each desired step can happen is different from asking whether all the steps would form a sustained cycle in one place without disruptive reactions. The laboratory case in the chapter raises a second question about provenance: where did the selected starting materials come from? A result with supplied inputs does not answer that prior question.

§VIThe gap between order and instructions

This section answers: Why does Lennox make information, rather than regularity alone, the next question?

Davies contrasts order imposed by boundary conditions with order directed by genetic information inside a living cell. Lennox says convection does not exemplify the language-like ordering of amino acids. Stephen Meyer argues that explaining how order arises does not explain how information arises.

Source DepthWhat Collins says about the available timeOptional source detail

What Collins says about the available time

Collins’s assessment specifies a window of 150 million years. He does not say that reasonable origin hypotheses have never been proposed, but says that no current hypothesis comes close to accounting for life’s emergence within that window and that the statistical prospect remains remote.

John C. Lennox, God’s Undertaker: Has Science Buried God?, ch. 7, pp. 133, 134.

Orgel allows several tenable accounts of the first organic material but finds the evidence uncompelling. He calls the hypothetical chemistry behind well-formulated replication scenarios problematic. Klaus Dose emphasizes the scale of the unresolved problem, Francis Crick the many conditions required, and Kauffman and Francis Collins that the origin is unknown. Lennox makes the origin of information the next subject.

Which explanatory task does each result address?
Convection cellsshowSpatial order formed under physical conditions
Chemical clockshowsRegular changes over time without a genetic code
Living cellusesInternal direction from encoded information, in Davies’s contrast
Checkpoint — Explain the chapter in three steps
  1. Name one common feature of known cells that contributes to Denton’s picture of basic biochemical uniformity.
  2. Separate the chance of selecting one handed form, the chance of linking a chain by the required bonds, and the chance of getting one specified order. What changes from one question to the next?
  3. Tell a partner what an oscillating reaction can show and what it cannot yet show. Then state how Orgel’s and Collins’s assessments keep Lennox’s final question open.

Revision Block · Dossier 3.4.9

Chapter Summary

Lennox starts with the gap between the regular patterns of nonliving matter and the coordinated work of known cells. Denton and Monod describe the underlying machinery shared by cells. Behe argues that some molecular machines point to design, while Lennox distinguishes that inference from the unsettled question of whether irreducibility has been established.

The discussion turns from the machinery to its origin. Experiments producing building blocks leave questions about the early atmosphere, molecular handedness, bonds, assembly time and ordering of sequences. The probability examples illustrate different tasks. Self-organization can produce repeating patterns, but Davies and Meyer distinguish these from genetically directed organization. The chapter ends with the origin of the first reproducer unresolved.

One-Page Revision Sheet

Cellular stasisDenton and Monod stress the shared underlying biochemical plan of known cells.
IrreducibilityBehe’s flagellum and mousetrap both ask whether removing a necessary part stops a specified function.
Two starting pointsDawkins begins with replication; Shapiro begins with energy-driven chemistry without heredity.
Miller and OparinA laboratory result under a chosen atmosphere is not a finding about what the early atmosphere was.
Two chemical constraintsOne handedness and peptide bonding have distinct roles in a chain that folds reproducibly.
ThermodynamicsThe statistical tendency of a closed system makes spontaneous assembly unlikely; it does not absolutely forbid it.
One sequenceOne specified order under the twenty-choice model is a different event from those earlier chemical constraints.
Self-organizationConvection organizes space; the chemical clock organizes repeated changes over time.
Orgel’s objectionA plausible isolated reaction is not proof that the necessary whole cycle would persist.
InformationFor Davies, cellular organization is directed by encoded instructions; convection is directed by external physical conditions.

Key Definitions

Irreducible complexity
In Behe’s usage, a system cannot effectively perform a basic function once a necessary interacting part is removed.
Replicator-first proposal
A copy-making molecule precedes the later organization of life.
Metabolism-first proposal
Chemical organization driven by energy precedes a mechanism of heredity.
Chirality
Handedness of mirror-image forms, called L and D in this discussion.
Peptide bond
The kind of link the chapter identifies between amino acids in a functional protein chain.
Protein sequence
The order in which amino acids occupy the positions of a chain.
Autocatalysis
A product participates in promoting its own further production.
Self-organization
The emergence of order from physical or chemical processes without genetic instructions in Lennox’s examples.
Genetically directed organization
Order in living things directed by genetic information, in Davies’s account.
Abiogenesis
The question of the origin of life from nonliving material, distinct from change within already reproducing life.
Prebiotic chemistry
Chemistry considered before a first living system is available to direct reactions.
Chemical clock
A reaction exhibiting regular changes over time, illustrated in the chapter by alternating colours.

Key Table — Three explanatory levels

Response to a proposed first-cell account
LevelQuestion to ask
MaterialsCan the proposed environment supply and preserve the required building blocks?
StructureHow are the building blocks bonded and arranged so that the chain can function?
Internal directionHow could the coded instructions that direct the living system arise?

Memory Aids Collected

  • Mousetrap: Choose the function under test before removing the component.
  • Davies’s bricks: Having energy available does not explain how construction is directed.
  • Balbus’s letters: Possessing an alphabet is not the same as arranging a verse.
  • Convection and code: The pattern of a fluid does not require the genetic directions that Davies attributes to a living cell.

Possible Examination Questions

Short Answer
  1. What do Denton and Monod regard as shared across known cells?
  2. What is chirality, and how is it distinct from the type of bond?
Long Answer
  1. Reconstruct the argument from Miller’s result to the difficulty of obtaining one specified sequence.
  2. Explain why Lennox considers self-organization but closes by turning to the origin of information.
Comparison
  1. Compare the replicator-first and metabolism-first proposals and identify where heredity enters each.
  2. Compare Behe’s design inference with Lennox’s statement of what remains disputed.
Conceptual
  1. Why is identifying a necessary reaction not enough to establish a whole cycle in Orgel’s argument?
  2. How do the calculations for handedness, bonds and a specified sequence differ in the thing counted?
Application
  1. A chemical pattern repeats reliably. Apply Davies’s distinction to explain what further evidence would be needed to treat it as an example of genetically directed order.
  2. Explain how the changed atmospheric assumptions affect the force of Miller’s result in Lennox’s argument.
